summary:
Ten Days on the Moon: Flare Alert is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12. The idea is simple: play first, then learn. Children usually meet space science in a textbook. Here they meet it as a problem they have to solve.

The player commands a small Moon outpost for ten days. There is not enough solar power to run everything, the crew has missions to finish, and the Sun in the game does what the real Sun did on those dates: every flare and particle storm is replayed from NASA's DONKI space weather records. When a flare alert arrives, the player has to decide, without knowing if a storm will follow, whether to keep the crew working outside or to call them in.

That decision is what makes a child curious. What is a flare? Why did a storm come this time? The answers are in a Field guide inside the game, which fills up with real space facts as the game goes on.

It runs in any browser, with no download and no account.
details:
The idea: play first, then learn. Children usually meet space science in a textbook. In this game they meet it as a decision they have to make, and the facts are there when they want to know why.

What it does. You are the commander of a Moon outpost for ten days. Each turn is one day: in the morning you give the orders, then you watch the day play out on a picture of the base seen from above.

Before the game you choose your crew: six astronauts, not enough seats. Each one has work they love and do better, one friend and one rival.

Every morning you share out the power and give everyone a job. The solar panels make about 7 units a day; running all six modules (Life Support, Greenhouse, Radio Dish, Sun Telescope, Lab, Rover Bay) would take 10. The crew can grow food, do research, build a radio telescope outside, repair solar panels, drive the rover, rest, go to the sick bay or call home.

When the Sun fires a flare, Mission Control calls, if your radio has power. Carry on and all the work gets done, but if a particle storm follows, anyone outside is badly hurt. Call the crew in and they lose half a day's work or more. Nobody dies in the game: if things go very wrong the crew flies home early and the player can try again. Every game starts a little differently.

The Field guide. Real-life facts are kept out of the play and collected in a Field guide inside the game: what a solar flare is, why only some flares send dangerous particles, Moon soil as a radiation shield, water ice at the Moon's south pole. It fills up as the game goes on, and each fact links to the NASA page it was checked against.

How it answers the challenge. The challenge names life support, radiation shielding, power, food production and communication. Each one is a real choice in the game, and they compete for the same power: air needs power every day; every flare alert is a choice about radiation; the Greenhouse needs power and care; and with the Radio Dish off, no alert reaches you. The game does not model the real signal delay to the Moon.

Real data. The flares and storms are not random. Three levels each replay ten real days from NASA's DONKI database: 1-10 December 2019 (no flares listed), 3-12 September 2017 (35 flares, particle storms began on 3 days) and 6-15 May 2024 (118 flares, particle storms began on 3 days). The game uses saved records, not live data, and says so on screen. A panel called "What is real in this game?" tells players what is real, what is simplified and what is made up.

How it was built. TypeScript, React and Vite. The rules are plain TypeScript with 69 automated tests, separate from the picture, which is drawn on an HTML canvas. A script downloads the records from the DONKI API, so anyone can regenerate the data. It is deployed on GitHub Pages and needs no server, no login and no download. The code was written with AI coding tools, directed and checked by the author; the README has a section called "Use of AI".
